diagnoses.preserve: KANs are presented as alternatives to MLPs; preserve both expanded names and abbreviations.
diagnoses.problem: “Promising” endorses KANs without identifying a capability, condition, or result that makes the endorsement useful.
diagnoses.quote: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) are promising alternatives of Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs).

diagnoses.preserve: The claimed comparison concerns edge versus node activations and both accuracy and interpretability; the stronger improvement is qualified by “sometimes.”
diagnoses.problem: The blanket causal comparison lacks task or evaluation conditions, while “simple” and “sometimes much better!” add promotional emphasis without a measure of improvement. Later discussion explicitly acknowledges setting-dependent advantages and limitations.
diagnoses.quote: This simple change makes KANs better (sometimes much better!) than MLPs in terms of both model

diagnoses.preserve: Call the protected speed method before training under the preceding conditions; otherwise the symbolic branch remains on, and its computations are not parallelized.
diagnoses.problem: “Super slow” and the exclamation marks amplify a performance warning without quantifying it. The nonparallelized symbolic computations already provide the concrete reason for the warning.
diagnoses.quote: Otherwise, the symbolic branch is on, which is super slow because the symbolic computations are not parallelized!

diagnoses.preserve: The section introduces advice about tuning KAN hyperparameters.
diagnoses.problem: This rhetorical question repeats the section heading and delays the useful explanation of the advice’s empirical basis and limited scope.
diagnoses.quote: So how can I tune the hyperparameters effectively?

diagnoses.preserve: The author intends the experience-based advice to help users choose a starting point and set expectations.
diagnoses.problem: The statement repeats the preceding announcement of personal advice and adds an extended statement of intent without another tuning instruction or caveat.
diagnoses.quote: But I want to at least share my experience such that users can have better clues where to start and what to expect from tuning hyperparameters.

diagnoses.preserve: Accuracy, interpretability, and parameter efficiency need not conflict; retain the Figure 2.3 reference and the later qualification that tradeoffs can occur.
diagnoses.problem: “I also want to emphasize” and the nested “and also” bury the substantive three-way relationship under announcement language.
diagnoses.quote: I also want to emphasize that accuracy and interpretability (and also parameter efficiency) are not necessarily contradictory, e.g., Figure 2.3 in

diagnoses.preserve: Recommend pursuing one goal at a time, subject to the following exception when pruning plausibly helps accuracy.
diagnoses.problem: “Not to be greedy” moralizes a technical choice, and “it would be good” adds an indirect lead-in to the actual prioritization advice.
diagnoses.quote: So it would be good not to be greedy and aim for one goal at a time.

diagnoses.preserve: After a satisfactory initial result, the author recommends increasing the dataset and performing a final run, with an expectation rather than a guarantee of improvement.
diagnoses.problem: “Quite good” and “even better results!” leave both the readiness criterion and expected improvement unspecified. The upbeat prediction also needs to remain consistent with the following caveat that small and large datasets may behave differently.
diagnoses.quote: Once you get a quite good result, try increasing data size and have a final run, which should give you even better results!

diagnoses.preserve: The simple-first approach reflects the author’s physics background and personal, potentially biased experience.
diagnoses.problem: “Quite effective” and “make things well-controlled” offer vague benefits, while the sentence generalizes a personal method to physicists as a group. The nearby debugging explanation supplies a more concrete benefit.
diagnoses.quote: Disclaimer: Try the simplest thing first is the mindset of physicists, which could be personal/biased but I find this mindset quite effective and make things well-controlled for me.

diagnoses.preserve: Users should continually check whether their model is underfitting or overfitting.
diagnoses.problem: “Another thing that would be good to keep in mind is that” postpones a concrete diagnostic instruction with empty reminder language.
diagnoses.quote: Another thing that would be good to keep in mind is that please constantly checking if your model is in underfitting or overfitting regime.

diagnoses.preserve: Start with a simple, initially underfitting model and expand it gradually toward a suitable fit, following the preceding overfitting checks.
diagnoses.problem: “This is also the reason why I'd love to” repeats the author’s preference, and the undefined “Goldilocks zone” makes the desired fitting regime less explicit than the surrounding technical terms.
diagnoses.quote: This is also the reason why I'd love to start from simple models to make sure that the model is first in underfitting regime and then gradually expands to the "Goldilocks zone".

diagnoses.preserve: For machine learning applications, KANs are likely not yet usable as a simple out-of-the-box plug-in.
diagnoses.problem: “I have to be honest” adds a sincerity announcement before an important usability caveat; it contributes no condition or explanation.
diagnoses.quote: For users who are machine learning focus, I have to be honest that KANs are likely not a simple plug-in that can be used out-of-the box (yet).

diagnoses.preserve: The author values LLM interpretability and cautions that interpretability can mean different things in LLMs and science.
diagnoses.problem: “Do,” “for sure,” and “wildly” pile emphasis onto the distinction without specifying how the meanings differ.
diagnoses.quote: We do care about LLM interpretability for sure, but interpretability can mean wildly different things for LLM and for science.

diagnoses.preserve: The author hopes the ideas will inspire further work without claiming they are necessarily the future; retain the concrete ideas of learnable edge activations and AI-assisted scientific discovery.
diagnoses.problem: The language about inspiring and impacting unspecified futures gives no concrete meaning to “impact” and extends a personal hope into a vague promotional conclusion.
diagnoses.quote: , but can hopefully inspire and impact

diagnoses.preserve: Empirical trials reveal whether approaches succeed or fail, including outcomes that cannot be known beforehand.
diagnoses.problem: This repeats the preceding practice-as-test maxim through an unspecified “many things”; “beforehand until” and “really tried and shown to be” add complexity without another testing criterion.
diagnoses.quote: We don't know many things beforehand until they are really tried and shown to be succeeding or failing.
